explanations.explanation: This neuron is signaling the boundary of the opening sentence (or title) of a text block—spiking strongly on the very first content word and again on the period that ends that first sentence.

This neuron fires on the “dot” of uppercase‐letter abbreviations or initials (e.g. C., St., Jan., U.S., Inc., Drs., A.W., etc.), the sentence‐internal periods that mark acronyms, titles, dateline abbreviations and similar shorthand.
This feature fires on the sentence-final full stop (the period), i.e. it marks the end-of-sentence boundary.

This feature is a structural‐boundary detector: it spikes on the first content word of a new sentence or heading (especially capitalized tokens like Den, Ama, Along, Every, Hen, Ber, Look, “Today,” “Acc–,” etc.) and on boundary punctuation (periods in abbreviations, dates or decimal numbers) that marks the edges of sentences or segments.
This feature fires on the “.” (period) token—e.g. after initials (J.), in abbreviations and acronyms (Inc., FFT.), domain names (site.com), and as a sentence‐ending dot.
This feature is a detector for the standalone “.” punctuation token—marking sentence-end periods, abbreviation dots (e.g. “M.”, “P.C.”), and decimal or numeric separators.

This neuron fires on the little “headline” or section‐starter words—i.e. the initial, often capitalized tokens that kick off titles, headings, list items or structural blocks (Used, Disc, For, From, Below, Real, Ep, WBAL, etc.), marking document structure rather than ordinary content.

This feature detects evaluative or attributional language—stative verbs and adjectives that express reputation, appearance, expectation or stance (e.g. “eager,” “famous,” “seems,” “supposed,” “known,” “excited”).

This feature detects the little “joiners” that bind multi‐word or split words into compounds or names—chiefly hyphens (including line-break hyphenation) and similar connectives (e.g. ampersands) marking internal word boundaries.

This feature is a detector for the “.” (full-stop/dot) token, regardless of whether it’s ending a sentence, marking abbreviations (e.g. “St.”, “No.”), serving as a decimal point (e.g. “50.00”), or starting an ellipsis.
